technique.how: After brief formal cognitive testing (orientation, digit span or months backwards) and collateral from nurse/family, score four features: (1) acute onset and fluctuating course, (2) inattention, (3) disorganized thinking, (4) altered level of consciousness. CAM positive = features 1 AND 2 plus either 3 or 4. Takes about 5 minutes.
technique.prerequisites: Collateral informant or nursing observations for the fluctuation item; the rater should be trained and score from observed cognitive testing rather than casual conversation.
technique.contraindications: None; use CAM-ICU in intubated/non-verbal patients.

interpretation.positive_finding: Delirium present (pooled LR+ about 9.6). Treat as an acute medical problem and search for precipitants (infection, drugs, metabolic, withdrawal, CNS).
interpretation.negative_finding: Delirium unlikely (pooled LR- about 0.16), though a negative screen at one time point does not exclude a fluctuating course; repeat if suspicion persists.
interpretation.pitfalls: Sensitivity falls sharply when scored without formal cognitive testing or by untrained raters. Hypoactive delirium and pre-existing dementia are the commonest sources of missed or false-positive results.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: launch a delirium precipitant work-up and non-drug management; negative: pursue non-delirium causes of the presentation, re-screen if course fluctuates.

estimates.population: Hospitalized adults, mostly older, across 25 prospective studies (N=3027)
estimates.reference_standard: DSM-based diagnosis by geriatrician, psychiatrist or neurologist
estimates.quote: the CAM has the best available supportive data as a bedside delirium instrument (summary-positive LR, 9.6; 95% CI, 5.8-16.0; summary-negative LR, 0.16;

estimates.population: Seven high-quality CAM validation studies (N=1071), mixed hospital populations
estimates.reference_standard: Expert clinical diagnosis against DSM criteria
estimates.quote: demonstrating an overall sensitivity of 94% (95% confidence interval (CI)=91-97%) and specificity of 89% (95% CI=85-94%)

sources.citation: Wong CL, Holroyd-Leduc J, Simel DL, Straus SE. Does this patient have delirium?: value of bedside instruments. JAMA 2010;304:779-786.
Wei LA, Fearing MA, Sternberg EJ, Inouye SK. The Confusion Assessment Method: a systematic review of current usage. J Am Geriatr Soc 2008;56:823-830.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a single negative CAM to exclude delirium in a patient with fluctuating alertness; do not use in intubated patients without the ICU adaptation.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A positive CAM with fever, meningism, focal deficit or reduced consciousness needs urgent infection/CNS work-up, not just delirium precautions.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Wei 2008 notes performance depends on training and on scoring from formal cognitive testing; untrained ad hoc use lowers sensitivity.

extraction_notes: Both estimates from abstracts (JAMA RCE not in PMC OA; JAGS not OA), so location is 'Abstract, Results'; RCE Table with per-study values not viewed. Pooled sens/spec (Wei 2008) and pooled LRs (Wong 2010) come from different study sets and are kept as separate entries. PMIDs confirmed.
